body.text: In recent years, Moscow’s official stance on North Korea’s denuclearization and sanctions has shifted: Russian diplomats now say denuclearization has become an irrelevant term and sanctions have proved ineffective. Both issues became part of Russia’s broader criticism of the United States’ policy.

Moscow’s skepticism of sanctions dates back to the 2000s. During the Six-Party Talks in 2003-2009, Russia argued that sanctions should persuade North Korea to maintain dialogue rather than punish it. After Pyongyang announced its exit from the Six-Party Talks in April 2009, Russia’s then-Vice Foreign Minister Alexey Borodavkin claimed participants would be better off discussing how to resume the multilateral format than strengthening sanctions.

When United Nations sanctions were tightened following North Korea’s second nuclear test in May 2010, Russia’s permanent representatives to the U.N. highlighted that the measures should not have negative humanitarian consequences and could be reversed if Pyongyang followed the resolution’s recommendations.

The sanctions regime on North Korea intensified in the 2010s, coinciding with the gradual deterioration of Russia–U.S. relations and Western countries’ introduction of sanctions on Russia. North Korea’s case was utilized to challenge the legitimacy of unilateral sanctions and the U.S.-initiated U.N. sanctions, as Russia’s Foreign Ministry and U.N. representatives began framing them as excessive and harmful to the humanitarian situation.

In 2017, Russian diplomats argued that sanctions did not achieve their security goal and caused a deterioration of living conditions in North Korea. While voicing concerns about sanctions’ effects, however, Russia still voted for their introduction, likely weighing China’s frustration with North Korea.

Relations with the United States and European countries deteriorated sharply since Russia’s invasion of Ukraine in 2022, and unilateral economic restrictions on Russia were imposed. Since then, Moscow has stepped up efforts to discredit Western sanctions.

After vetoing the resolution extending the mandate of the 1718 Committee Panel of Experts in 2024, Russia’s Permanent Representative to the U.N. Vasily Nebenzya argued that the Panel of Experts’ work had been reduced to playing up to the West in recent years. Nebenzya claimed that North Korea’s legitimate activities had become a target of the Washington-led coalition’s pressure.

Given North Korea’s importance to China, Russia’s decision to veto the resolution extending the mandate of the 1718 Committee Panel of Experts in 2024 was likely coordinated with Chinese counterparts, rather than made unilaterally. Although the United States and its allies launched the Multilateral Sanctions Monitoring Team (MSMT) to compensate for the loss of the Panel of Experts, Russia has stressed its illegitimacy, as it had no U.N. mandate. In 2026, Nebenzya claimed that MSMT’s reports were mere fabrications and disinformation.

The shifts in Russia’s official discourse on North Korea’s nuclear program are even more profound, evolving from firm condemnation of Pyongyang’s nuclear ambitions to acknowledgment of its self-defense measures as fully legitimate. A distinction should be made between North Korea’s nuclear and missile programs: while Moscow used to oppose Pyongyang’s nuclear tests, it never portrayed North Korean missile development as a threat. Russia’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs issued protests each time North Korea conducted nuclear tests in 2006, 2009, 2013, 2016, and 2017. The statements consistently highlighted that these actions pose a serious threat to peace and security on the Korean Peninsula and across the Asia-Pacific region, with negative consequences for Pyongyang.

After signing the 2024 Comprehensive Strategic Partnership agreement, Russia’s official rhetoric on North Korea’s denuclearization changed. In September 2024, Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov stressed that it was a “closed issue” for Russia, highlighting that denuclearization had lost meaning given the intensifying South Korea-U.S. military alliance. Visiting North Korea in summer 2025, he stated that Russia respects Pyongyang’s actions and understands the reasons why it carries out its nuclear program. Lavrov explicitly cited the US and South Korea’s military exercises and the 2023 Washington Declaration that allowed Seoul to participate in information sharing and consultations regarding nuclear contingencies as an explanation for increasing tension on the Korean Peninsula.

Similarly, in November 2026, Foreign Ministry Spokeswoman Maria Zakharova argued that Russia sees North Korea’s efforts to boost its defense capabilities “as entirely legitimate and justified, fully consistent with the right of self-defense enshrined in the U.N. Charter.” While this tacit acknowledgment of Pyongyang’s nuclear program challenges the NPT and the IAEA’s authority, Moscow frames its stance and North Korea’s policies as legitimate by selectively applying existing norms and interpreting international law in its own way.

Russia’s evolving approach to Pyongyang’s nuclear program and related sanctions is just one episode of its broader attempts to contest existing norms and challenge the United States’ foreign policy. It is also an example of Moscow’s effort to question the rules-based order, which it sees as imposed by Western countries without consideration of the interests of the Global South.

This line of criticism goes back to the late 2010s. In 2017, Lavrov argued that the West tries to replace the rule of law in international affairs with a rules-based order, suggesting that the Western interpretation of international law does not equal the law itself. As ambiguities in international law continue to expand and the international system becomes more polarized, more cases like North Korea may arise, where existing norms are contested.
